terms.short: Restore the person to the research
Restore the actor to the action
Restore the motive to the metric
Restore the labour and the material
Restore the consequence to the decision

titles.note: Accepted to get in. Rarely read.
Fluency, as a condition of entry.
People, defined by what they do for the product.

users.r: people, named by what they do for the product

segments.r: people grouped by their value to the business

algorithm.r: a system a team built, tunes and maintains

friction.r: harm, renamed as a routine operation

consent.r: the people who did not refuse, counted

churn.r: a person who tried to leave

cloud.r: water, land, minerals, heat and labour

n1.label: Note 1
n1.text: Don Norman, who named user experience, wrote in 2008: “Time to wipe words such as consumer, customer, and user from our vocabulary.”

n2.label: Note 2
n2.text: Langdon Winner argued in 1980 that artefacts can embody politics. The vocabulary that specifies an artefact is part of it.

n3.label: Note 3
n3.text: Susan Leigh Star describes infrastructure as “learned as part of membership” and as something that “becomes visible upon breakdown.” A new designer learns the vocabulary as the price of belonging.

n4.label: Note 4
n4.text: GDPR, Article 7(3): “It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.”

n5.label: Note 5
n5.text: Design Justice Network, principle 2: “We center the voices of those who are directly impacted by the outcomes of the design process.”

n6.label: Note 6
n6.text: Feminist Data Manifest-No, 9: “We refuse a data regime of ultimatums, coercive permissions, pervasive cookie collecting, and blocked access.”

n7.label: Note 7
n7.text: Mierle Laderman Ukeles, Manifesto for Maintenance Art, 1969: “after the revolution, who’s going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?”

dxd.label: Definition
dxd.text: Digital experience design: designing websites, apps and services as whole experiences, across research, interaction, content and interface, usually inside a product team.

analytics.label: Definition
analytics.text: Analytics: software that records and reports how people use a product, such as Google Analytics or Amplitude. It decides what counts as a user, a session and a success.

designsystems.label: Definition
designsystems.text: Design system: a shared library of components, patterns and writing rules that a company publishes so every team builds the same way. Google’s Material Design is one.

tickets.label: Definition
tickets.text: Ticket: a unit of work in a tracker such as Jira that tells a team exactly what to build next.

components.label: Definition
components.text: Component: a reusable interface element, such as a button or a banner, defined once and repeated across a product.

releasenotes.label: Definition
releasenotes.text: Release note: the published summary of what changed in a product update.

dataprotection.label: Definition
dataprotection.text: Data protection law: rules such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (2018) that set conditions for collecting and using personal data, including valid consent.

platformcap.label: Definition
platformcap.text: Platform capitalism: Nick Srnicek’s term for an economy in which firms profit by owning the digital platforms that other people’s activity passes through.

growthmetrics.label: Definition
growthmetrics.text: Growth metrics: the numbers a business tracks to show it is expanding, such as sign-ups, active users and revenue per person.

words.replacement: the people who did not refuse, counted
words.why: The GDPR defines consent as “freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous.” A rate measures completed acceptance, not any of those conditions.
words.honest: The goal changes: refusal made easy, not acceptance made higher.

words.replacement: agree to what you have not read
words.why: GDPR Article 7(3): “It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.” The banner layout decides whether it is.
words.honest: Refuse gets the same size, colour and position as accept.

words.why: Google Analytics measures it as “the amount of time someone spends with your web page in focus.” The time is counted. Whether it was wanted is not.
words.honest: Success becomes time people wanted, not time held.

words.replacement: harm, renamed as a routine operation
words.why: Cox and colleagues argue design frictions can “disrupt ‘mindless’ automatic interactions, prompting moments of reflection.” Some friction is the care.
words.honest: Protective pauses stop being tickets to remove.
words.source: Cox et al., Design Frictions for Mindful Interactions, CHI 2016

words.why: The site that named them now says: “This website was formerly called ‘Dark Patterns’ (darkpatterns.org).” The new name says what the pattern does.
words.honest: Named as deception, it stops reading as a style choice.

words.replacement: a person, named by what they do for the product
words.why: Don Norman, who named user experience, wrote in 2008: “Time to wipe words such as consumer, customer, and user from our vocabulary.”
words.honest: Research asks who people are, not what they do for the product.

words.replacement: a person who tried to leave
words.why: Amplitude: “Churn is the percentage of customers, users, or revenue lost from a business.” People and revenue, in one clause, lost from the business.
words.honest: Leaving becomes a flow to design well, not a loss to prevent.

words.replacement: water, land, minerals, heat and labour
words.why: Li and colleagues estimate that training GPT-3 in Microsoft’s US data centres could directly evaporate 700,000 litres of clean freshwater. The cloud is on the ground.
words.honest: Water, energy and location enter the brief and the report.
words.source: Li, Yang, Islam & Ren, Making AI Less ‘Thirsty’, 2023

words.replacement: work done by people you do not see
words.why: Sarah T. Roberts documents the commercial content moderators who screen what platforms show: human work presented as automatic.
words.honest: Moderation and labelling are credited, costed and cared for.
words.source: Roberts, Behind the Screen, Yale University Press, 2019

words.why: Puschmann and Burgess trace big data framed first as a force of nature, then as a resource: “the natural force turns into a natural resource to be consumed.”
words.honest: Collection needs a purpose and a limit, not a yield.
words.source: Puschmann & Burgess, Metaphors of Big Data, 2014

words.why: Nick Seaver reads recommender systems through the anthropology of animal traps, where the purpose is captivation.
words.honest: Recommendation goals shift from time held to needs met.

words.replacement: records of people’s lives, treated as waste
words.why: Shoshana Zuboff describes human experience claimed as “free raw material for translation into behavioural data”. Exhaust implies waste. It is the product.
words.honest: Behavioural data is treated as people’s, with limits on its use.
words.source: Zuboff, The Age of Surveillance Capitalism, 2019 (quoted via Wikipedia)

words.why: Eric Meyer and Sara Wachter-Boettcher designed for stress cases instead: “Common human experiences aren’t ‘edge’ cases.”
words.honest: People under stress move from the backlog into the core flows.
words.source: Meyer & Wachter-Boettcher, Design for Real Life, 2016

words.why: Google Ads: “An impression is counted each time your ad is shown.” Shown, not seen.
words.honest: Reports separate shown from seen.

words.replacement: a person persuaded to pay or agree
words.why: Google now calls the underlying event a key event: “an action that’s particularly important to the success of your business.” Whose success is in the definition.
words.honest: Reports record how people were brought to the outcome.
words.source: Google Analytics Help, About key events

words.why: Chalmers and MacColl argued for “seamful” design: showing a system’s seams so people can understand its limits and work with them.
words.honest: The seams where decisions sit are shown, not hidden.
words.source: Chalmers & MacColl, Seamful and Seamless Design in Ubiquitous Computing, 2003

words.why: AWS: “build and run applications and services without thinking about servers.” Not thinking about them is the product. They are still there.
words.honest: Where it runs, and on whose infrastructure, is stated.

words.why: Couldry and Mejias name it data colonialism: how data is “colonizing human life and appropriating it for capitalism.”
words.honest: Markets are described as places people already live.
words.source: Couldry & Mejias, The Costs of Connection, 2019

words.replacement: built in, or born to a place
words.why: Google’s word list: “Avoid using native to refer to people. When referring to software products, try to use a more precise term — for example, use built-in.”
words.honest: Products say built-in. People are never native to a platform.

words.why: GitHub made main the default branch name for new repositories from October 2020. A default changed at platform scale.
words.honest: Nothing, now. It was already changed.

words.why: Google’s word list: “Don’t use blacklist, whitelist, and graylist. Instead, use more precise terms that are appropriate for your domain.”
words.honest: Nothing, now. It was already changed.

words.why: Google: “Avoid when possible. Instead, use words like stop, exit, cancel, or end.” The violence in a verb about a process was ruled on. The nouns that replace a person were not.
words.honest: Nothing, now. It was already changed.
